summary: OCSP requires signed responses but didn't say how to choose the signature algorithm. This standards-track document defines rules for server selection and an extension for clients to indicate preferences. It was replaced by RFC 6960.

eli5.summary: When checking a certificate is still good, the answer must be signed, and the two sides now agree on which signing style. It was later replaced by RFC 6960.

how does ocsp client request algorithm
subtitle: Letting OCSP clients and servers agree on signature algorithms for certificate status responses.

tldr.problem: OCSP requires signed responses to certificate status queries, but the original standard did not specify how to choose which signature algorithm to use, leading to interoperability failures when clients and servers support different algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies rules for servers to select a signature algorithm and defines an extension that lets clients indicate their preferred algorithms.
tldr.outcome: OCSP implementations can now negotiate signature algorithms reliably, ensuring that servers generate responses clients can verify. RFC 6277 was replaced by RFC 6960.

today: RFC 6277 is now Historic, having been replaced by RFC 6960, which provides a consolidated specification of OCSP with updated algorithm requirements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) [RFC 2560] provides a way to check whether an X.509 certificate is still valid in real time. An OCSP responder receives a request for the status of a certificate and must return a signed response. However, the original specification left the choice of signature algorithm undefined, requiring only that clients support DSA and optionally support RSA.

In practice, OCSP responders may have different cryptographic capabilities than the certification authority that issued the certificate being checked. A responder might prefer to use RSA with SHA-256 for security reasons, while a client might only support RSA with SHA-1. Without a way to communicate these preferences, responders could generate responses that clients cannot verify, causing the certificate check to fail.
sections.eli5: When your browser checks if a certificate is still good, a server has to sign the answer. But nobody said which signing method to use. If the server and browser pick different methods, the answer will not work.

sections.title: The Problem: Algorithm Disagreement
sections.content:
Although OCSP allowed responders to choose from multiple signature algorithms, no mechanism existed for clients to indicate which algorithms they support. This created several failure scenarios.

If a responder always selected the same algorithm used to sign the certificate being checked, this could fail when a responder signs its own responses with a different key type. For example, a CA might use RSA signatures for certificates but the OCSP responder might use ECDSA for its responses, which older clients would not recognize.

When a responder received a request for an unknown certificate, it had no basis for choosing an algorithm at all. Without in-band signaling from the client, the responder had to guess, often leading to a mismatch. Some responders computed pre-signed responses in advance, making dynamic algorithm selection impossible.
sections.eli5: The server might want to sign with algorithm A, but the client only knows algorithm B. Without a way to communicate, the server just guesses, and often gets it wrong.

sections.title: Mandatory Algorithms and Client Preferences
sections.content:
This document updates RFC 2560 to specify which algorithms all OCSP clients and responders must support. Clients MUST be able to process responses signed with RSA with SHA-1 and RSA with SHA-256, and SHOULD also support DSA with SHA-1. Other algorithms MAY be supported.

The document defines a new extension called PreferredSignatureAlgorithms that clients MAY include in their OCSP requests. This extension contains an ordered list of signature algorithms the client prefers, from most to least preferred. The client specifies not only the signature algorithm (e.g., ECDSA with SHA-256) but optionally also the public key algorithm the client expects in the responder's certificate (e.g., the specific elliptic curve to use).

A client MUST only list algorithms it actually supports and MUST accept any algorithm it lists in the preferred set when it receives the response.
sections.eli5: All OCSP clients must understand RSA with SHA-1 and SHA-256. A client can send a list of algorithms it prefers, in order. The server tries to use the client's first choice, then the second, and so on.

sections.title: Responder Algorithm Selection
sections.content:
When a responder receives an OCSP request, it selects a signature algorithm using the following priority order.

First, if the request includes the PreferredSignatureAlgorithms extension, the responder SHOULD select the first algorithm from that list that it supports and that meets its security requirements. Second, if no preferred algorithm matches, the responder MAY use the signature algorithm that the certification authority used to sign the certificate's revocation list (CRL). Third, the responder MAY use the algorithm employed to sign the OCSP request itself. Fourth, the responder MAY use a default algorithm advertised out-of-band by the OCSP service. Finally, the responder MAY fall back to a mandatory or recommended algorithm for OCSP.

For pre-computed static responses, a responder cannot examine the request during generation but SHOULD still select the response to return based on matching the client's request properties. Responders MAY use historical client requests to decide which algorithm variations to pre-generate.
sections.eli5: The server checks the client's preference list first, then tries the algorithm the CA used, then the algorithm from the request, then a configured default, and finally a standard algorithm. It picks the first one it can do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The signature algorithm chosen MUST be sufficiently secure against cryptanalytic attack. In most cases, the signature algorithm should be at least as secure as the algorithm used to sign the original certificate.

The PreferredSignatureAlgorithms extension is not protected against man-in-the-middle downgrade attacks: an attacker could modify the request to remove stronger algorithms from the preference list. However, this is not a significant concern because OCSP responders MUST NOT sign responses using weak algorithms even if requested, and clients can reject responses that do not meet their own security criteria.

In some applications, such as long-term certificate archival, the algorithm used to sign a certificate on a specific date in the past may no longer be considered secure today. A responder MUST NOT generate a signature using an algorithm it considers insecure, even if that was the algorithm used when the certificate was originally signed.

Including the PreferredSignatureAlgorithms extension introduces a minor increase in the attack surface for denial-of-service attacks, where a client request could specify algorithms the server does not support, forcing expensive processing.
sections.eli5: Responders must refuse to use weak algorithms, even if a client asks for them. Clients can double-check the response meets their needs. Attackers could try to trick servers by modifying preferences, but servers check security independently.
